answer:
HYPOTHESIS (final, data-grounded): Between 1990 and 1996, within-group wealth inequality among white males and white females in the NLSY79 cohort DECREASED, and the male–female inequality gap NARROWED to near parity — as measured by composite_wealth_1990 and composite_wealth_1996 restricted to respondents with positive wealth, the treatment most defensible given that ~43% of white 1996 zeros are missing/nonresponse coding (23.1% of white males and 25.9% of white females with 1990 composite wealth ≥ $100,000 show exactly 0 in 1996, as do 22.5%/25.1% of those ≥ $250,000 — implausible as true total asset loss).

(a) White males (n=2,452 in 1990, 1,900 in 1996 with positive wealth): Gini fell from 0.688 to 0.623 (−0.066, −9.6%); P90/P50 fell from 5.7 to 3.9 (−31.5%); P90/P10 fell from 68.2 to 51.1 (−25.1%); top-20%/bottom-20% mean ratio fell from 102 to 71 (−30.4%); coefficient of variation fell from 2.25 to 1.65 (−26.9%).

(b) White females (n=2,713 in 1990, 2,016 in 1996): declines were somewhat larger — Gini 0.681 to 0.599 (−0.082, −12.0%); P90/P50 4.9 to 3.7 (−23.5%); P90/P10 84.0 to 55.3 (−34.1%); top-20%/bottom-20% 125 to 70 (−44.2%); CV 2.22 to 1.60 (−28.1%).

Compression came from the bottom: positive-wealth medians rose from $48,100 to $131,500 (+173%) for males and $58,400 to $132,000 (+126%) for females, outpacing the 90th percentile ($273K→$511K, +87% male; $286K→$494K, +73% female), while means rose +92% (male) and +73% (female).

(c) Male–female gap: in 1990 white females were more unequal than white males on ratio metrics (top-20%/bottom-20% 125 vs 102; P90/P10 84 vs 68) with Gini nearly equal (0.681 vs 0.688); by 1996 the groups were nearly identical (Gini 0.623 vs 0.599; top-20%/bottom-20% 71.2 vs 69.7; P90/P50 3.89 vs 3.74) — the female-leaning inequality gap closed. The wealth-level gap also narrowed and flipped: females had higher mean/median positive wealth in 1990 ($134,350 vs $125,590 mean; $58,400 vs $48,100 median); by 1996 means were nearly equal and slightly male-leaning ($241,193 vs $232,537) and medians nearly equal ($131,500 vs $132,000).

Caveat (treatment dependence, stated explicitly): if the 1996 zeros are instead treated as true zero wealth (winsorized full sample), the Gini INCREASED for both groups (male 0.674→0.745, +10.6%; female 0.655→0.740, +13.0%) and full-sample medians appear to fall ($15,601→$8,900 male; $20,100→$8,825 female). The positive-wealth reading is preferred because the exact-zero pattern among 1990 high-wealth respondents indicates missing coding, not true zero wealth; the full-sample 1990 Gini baseline is additionally distorted by extreme negative outliers (dropping the single −$866,400 row moves the 1990 female Gini from 0.080 to 0.397).

payload.hypothesis: Between 1990 and 1996, within-group wealth inequality among white males and white females in the NLSY79 cohort decreased, and the male-female inequality gap narrowed to near parity. Using composite_wealth_1990 and composite_wealth_1996 restricted to respondents with positive wealth (the most defensible treatment, since ~43% of white 1996 zeros are missing/nonresponse coding - 23.1% of white males and 25.9% of white females with 1990 wealth >= $100,000 show exactly 0 in 1996): (a) white males' Gini fell 0.688 -> 0.623 (-9.6%), P90/P50 fell 5.7 -> 3.9 (-31.5%), top-20%/bottom-20% mean ratio fell 102 -> 71 (-30.4%); (b) white females' Gini fell 0.681 -> 0.599 (-12.0%), P90/P50 fell 4.9 -> 3.7 (-23.5%), top-20%/bottom-20% fell 125 -> 70 (-44.2%); compression came from the bottom, with positive-wealth medians rising +173% (male, $48,100->$131,500) and +126% (female, $58,400->$132,000), outpacing the P90 (+87% male, +73% female). (c) In 1990 white females were more unequal than white males (top-20%/bottom-20% 125 vs 102; P90/P10 84 vs 68; Gini near-equal 0.681 vs 0.688); by 1996 the groups were nearly identical (Gini 0.623 vs 0.599; top-20%/bottom-20% 71.2 vs 69.7), so the female-leaning inequality gap closed; the wealth-level gap also narrowed and flipped slightly male-leaning on the mean ($241,193 vs $232,537 in 1996 vs $125,590 vs $134,350 in 1990). Caveat: if 1996 zeros are treated as true zero wealth (winsorized full sample), Ginis instead rose (male 0.674->0.745; female 0.655->0.740), so the direction is treatment-dependent; the zero-coding evidence favors the positive-wealth reading.
payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows x 6 columns, zero missing values); subset to race=='white' (male n=3,469; female n=3,630); compared composite_wealth_1990 vs composite_wealth_1996. Computed distributions (mean, median, SD, percentiles, zero/negative shares) and inequality metrics (Gini, coefficient of variation, P90/P10, P90/P50, top-20%/bottom-20% mean ratio on the positive subsample, mean/median) under four treatments: V1 full sample (zeros and negatives kept; Gini shifted), V2 positive wealth only (wealth > 0), V3 winsorized 1st-99th percentile, V4 exact-duplicate rows dropped (1,899 duplicates). Computed 1990->1996 change per group x metric x treatment, and male-minus-female gaps per metric at each wave plus the change in each gap. Robustness: excluded ever_jailed==1 (no material change) and V4 dedup (no material change). Verified zero-coding artifact (share of 1990 high-wealth respondents exactly 0 in 1996) and the V1 1990 Gini outlier artifact (single -866,400 row). Honest limitations: the file has no person-level ID, so this is a between-wave distributional comparison, NOT within-person change analysis; no sampling weights were provided (unweighted analysis); the composite wealth variable is a sum of five NLS components whose definitions are unavailable; the sample is the NLSY79 1958-1964 birth cohort (ages ~26-38 in these waves), not representative of all white US adults.
